gap: No blockquote rule. A draws a 3px #BFBFBF vertical bar at x=644 spanning the whole quote; B carries the quote on a single grey '>' on line one, so the wrapped second line is typographically indistinguishable from a plain indented paragraph. B's markers are also darker than A's heading hashes — grey 122 (~#7A, ~4.6:1 on #F9F9F9) vs A's 158 (~#A5, ~2.6:1) — so the ## reads as content rather than scaffolding.
gapTheirs: Markers are inline, so the text column moves between block types: body starts at x=682, H1 text 729, H2 text 747, bullet text 729, ordered text 747 — five left edges spanning 65px (~2.7 characters). Worse, the blockquote's second line starts at 676 while its first line starts at 730: a 54px leftward jog inside one quote, i.e. no hanging indent at all. B holds every block's text at 675–682 (7px spread, sub-glyph sidebearing) with markers outdented into a 602–631 gutter.
verdict: A's syntax is quieter per-glyph but it pays for that by shoving your prose around: every time you type '## ' the sentence you're writing slides 65px right, and a quote that wraps snaps back under its own '>'. That's the thing you feel at 2am — the left edge won't hold still, so nothing scans as a column and you re-find your place after every block. B outdents the markers into a gutter and keeps one text edge for headings, quotes, bullets and numbers alike, which is the entire reason to render markup inline instead of hiding it; it just forgot to keep the quote bar, and its markers at #7A are about 40% too present. B wins on the axis that actually costs writing time.

states.name: dark
states.gap: The blockquote gets no treatment beyond a grey '>' — no rule, no indent, no tint, no italic: B draws a 2px × 72px (CSS) rule in #404040 sitting 23px left of the quote text, while A's quote body is pixel-identical in colour, size and left edge (x=673) to an ordinary paragraph. A's caret is also #1C1C1C, the exact hex of body text, at 2px wide and 27px tall, versus B's 3px cyan bar at full 36px line-height.
states.gapTheirs: Markers sit inline instead of hanging, so the text's left edge jitters: paragraph text starts at x=673, H1 text at 721, H2 text at 747, bullet items at 722, quote line 1 at 721 — and that quote's own wrapped second line snaps back to 675, a 23px (CSS) step inside a single block. A holds every line — heading, body, quote, bullet, number, wrap — on one edge at 673–675, with all markers hung out into a 601–630 gutter.
states.verdict: A hangs '#', '##', '>', '-' and '1.' into the margin so the prose column never moves; B lets each marker shove its own line right by one to three characters, so the page has a ragged left edge that shifts every time you change block type, and the blockquote visibly breaks alignment with its own wrap. That is the thing you feel at the third hour: in B your eye has to re-find the start of the line, in A it lands in the same place every time. B buys back a hairline quote rule and a cyan 3px caret that A badly needs, but a caret you can find does not compensate for a column that will not stand still — and B's caret butts the following comma with 0px clearance, half-occluding it. Neither app scales a heading by a single pixel, so the outline is carried entirely by bold weight in both; A at least makes the markers do structural work.
